analysis.one_liner: Requires a vote of Congress before major federal regulations can take effect, and lets Congress revoke existing ones.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to two House committees on June 18, 1998 and sent to a subcommittee six days later, it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under this bill, any rule an agency proposes that Congress designates 'significant' could not take effect until both the House and Senate passed a joint resolution containing the rule's exact text, word for word. Agencies would have to file detailed reports with cost-benefit analyses before each such rule, and a special fast-track procedure would force a vote within 90 days — with no amendments allowed. Existing rules could also be revised or revoked if a petition signed by 120 House members or 30 senators asked for it. Rules on Federal Reserve monetary policy were excluded.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries facing costly federal rules gain a powerful new veto point: a regulation they oppose never takes effect if either chamber simply declines to pass it, and existing protections can be unwound through member petitions. The bill's sponsors framed it as democratic accountability — elected representatives, not unelected agency staff, deciding the terms of major rules — which also benefits voters who want Congress to own the rules made in its name.

how_it_helps.text: No 'significant' rule could take effect until Congress enacted a joint resolution containing the rule's exact text, giving elected lawmakers final approval over major regulations instead of agencies [S2][S3].

Agencies would have to submit the proposed rule, a summary of its purpose and effects, a complete cost-benefit analysis, and an explanation of the statutory interpretation behind it before it could become final [S2][S3].

The bill included special procedures designed to guarantee a floor vote: committees had to report the resolution within 45 days or be automatically discharged, a vote had to occur within 90 days, debate was limited, and amendments were banned [S3].
Existing rules could be revised or revoked through a petition process — 120 House members or 30 senators could force a vote on rescinding a rule they opposed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost whenever protections against polluted air and water, unsafe workplaces, unsafe products, financial misconduct, or other harms depend on rules that Congress now must affirmatively approve. Because Congress often cannot agree on anything, many rules would simply never take effect, and a bloc of 120 House members could force a vote to repeal an existing protection. Agencies would also carry new reporting duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: People who rely on federal safeguards

drawbacks.text: Requiring a full congressional vote for each major rule would likely stall most of them: Congress historically struggles to pass legislation on individual regulations, so the practical effect would be that many significant rules never take effect at all [S3].

The petition process for revoking existing rules would let a relative handful of members — 120 in the House — force votes to unwind protections, creating a standing channel for regulated interests to press their allies in Congress [S3].

The bill bars courts and agencies from inferring any intent of Congress from its failure to approve a rule, which would complicate legal challenges and remove one signal courts use to interpret statutes [S3].

The definition of 'significant rule' covers only rules that Congress expressly designates as such in the authorizing statute, so the regime's reach would depend entirely on what future laws choose to subject to it — a narrower scope than the bill's title suggests [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is real: Congress writes laws and delegates the details to agencies, and requiring a vote would force lawmakers to own the results. But the likely consequence is that important public protections — environmental, workplace, consumer, and financial — would stall or die by default, because Congress rarely acts affirmatively on individual rules, while a 120-member petition could target existing ones for repeal. The bill's design gives regulated parties structural leverage far beyond what its review-and-report requirements provide the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary and Rules committees, then to a Judiciary subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the 105th Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Smith of Michigan introduced the bill on June 18, 1998, with Reps. John Peterson and Ernest Istook as cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Rules Committee for provisions under their jurisdiction [S5].
On June 24, 1998, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, where it stayed [S5].

The committee never reported the bill, the House never voted on it, and no action of any kind followed after the subcommittee referral; the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing regulatory system stayed intact — agencies retained the power to issue and enforce rules without case-by-case congressional approval, and the industries that would have gained a veto point and a repeal channel got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the rules already on the books

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored, but the bill never reached a vote, so there is no record of how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Regulated industries generally (manufacturing, energy, finance, and other businesses subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would have given any significant rule a congressional approval gate — meaning a rule an industry opposed could be killed simply by Congress not acting — and a 120-member petition could force votes to repeal existing rules. The practical effect would be to shift regulatory fights into Congress, where concentrated interests are strongest, at the expense of the public protections those rules provide.

Agencies would face new reporting and cost-benefit duties, and their rules could no longer take effect without an act of Congress, weakening their capacity to carry out the laws they administer. The bill also excluded Federal Reserve monetary policy decisions entirely.
